solutions.check: 31 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Drunk – shown by Sun twice in black and white?

indicators.note: 'in' places one thing inside another, so one set of letters sits within the other

blocks.note: pied means patched in black and white, like a magpie
S is the abbreviation for Sunday, written twice

explanation.surface: Someone the worse for drink is caught out by a tabloid photo on two successive Sundays.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sun' looks like the newspaper, but it is the day's abbreviation; two Sundays sit inside the magpie's colouring.
explanation.definitionFit: Pissed is everyday British slang for intoxicated by alcohol, not the American sense of angry.

clue.text: Be presumptuous and outspoken, wearing mink?

definitions.note: loosely: to infer is to presume, to draw a conclusion

indicators.note: outspoken words are spoken out loud, so we go by how the phrase is pronounced

blocks.note: someone wearing mink is dressed in fur

explanation.surface: A brash, opinionated person flaunts a mink coat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In fur' said aloud sounds like the verb; the definition is a stretch, reading 'presume' as 'conclude'.
explanation.definitionFit: To presume something is to assume or conclude it, which is what inferring from evidence means.

clue.text: Scream "Gum!" being involved in an untidy struggle with some groping

definitions.text: an untidy struggle with some groping

indicators.note: things that get involved are tangled together, so the letters are mixed up

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone yells an exclamation of surprise while caught up in a messy, handsy tussle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gum!' is an old exclamation ('by gum'), here just letters; both words are mixed together.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrummage, like a rugby scrum, is a disorderly crowded tussle where bodies grapple and grab at each other.

clue.text: Pulling doctor above a hospital extension

indicators.note: in a down clue, what is above comes first, so the pieces are stacked in the stated order

blocks.note: DR is the usual abbreviation for doctor
taken as written
a wing is an extension of a hospital building

explanation.surface: A medic is chatting someone up, upstairs from a new hospital annexe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulling' suggests British slang for picking someone up; here it simply means hauling.
explanation.definitionFit: Drawing a cart or curtain is hauling or tugging it along, a plain synonym of the verb.

clue.text: New rota imposed on financial centre is an outrage

indicators.note: something new is a fresh version, so these letters take a different order
in an across clue, laid on top of means placed before, setting the order of pieces

blocks.note: the letters of the work schedule, rearranged
the City is London's financial district

explanation.surface: Bankers are furious that a new staff schedule has been forced on them.
explanation.walkthrough: The City, capitalised in speech, is the Square Mile of London where the banks are.
explanation.definitionFit: An atrocity is a shocking, wicked act that provokes moral indignation, which is what an outrage also means.

clue.text: (& 15/24) Steer clear of particular offspring, as an interrogated politician tends to do

definitions.text: as an interrogated politician tends to do
definitions.note: a description of the behaviour rather than a strict synonym

blocks.note: to steer clear of something is to keep away from it
the definite article picks out one particular thing
issue is a formal word for children

explanation.surface: Keeping away from your own child is mocked as typical of a politician being grilled.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase runs across three lights (5, 15 and 24 down). 'Issue' in its legal sense means children, so a literal reading is shunning one's kids.
explanation.definitionFit: Politicians under questioning famously dodge the topic raised, sidestepping the matter rather than answering it directly.

clue.text: Rose and Mabel screwed in posh car?

indicators.note: something screwed up is twisted out of shape, so these letters are contorted into a new order
'in' puts one thing inside another, so the shuffled letters go within the other piece

blocks.note: RR is short for Rolls-Royce, the classic posh car
the name's letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Two women, Rose and Mabel, have a fling in the back of a luxury car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rose' reads as a woman's name alongside Mabel, but it is the flower; 'screwed' has a ruder surface meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: A rambler is a type of climbing rose with long flexible stems, so it is an example of the flower.

clue.text: Chuck getting head from escort – class!

indicators.note: the head of a word is its first letter, so only the opening letter is kept

blocks.note: to chuck is to throw, as is to cast
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A man called Chuck receives oral sex from an escort, and someone cries 'Class!' in approval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chuck' poses as a name; it is the verb 'throw'. 'Getting head' is the setter's smutty disguise for taking a first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A caste is a hereditary social rank, as in the Indian system, so it is a kind of social class.

clue.text: Chunter on about staff

indicators.note: 'about' can mean all around and in disorder, so the letters are scattered and reformed

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles on and on about the employees.
explanation.walkthrough: To chunter is a British word for mutter or grumble. 'Staff' looks like employees, but it means a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A truncheon is a short club carried by police, and a staff is likewise a stout stick used as a weapon.

clue.text: Right-wing pundit, without right ball, is a right mess

indicators.note: 'without' in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps around another

blocks.note: Nigel Farage, the right-wing British politician and broadcaster
R is the standard abbreviation for right
O is round, like a ball

explanation.surface: A rude jibe that a right-wing commentator is missing a testicle and is a total shambles.
explanation.walkthrough: The name goes around R, and its last letter gives way to the round O; the parse is loose, with 'without' doing the wrapping.
explanation.definitionFit: A farrago is a confused jumble or hotchpotch, so in British slang it is a proper muddle.

clue.text: Cyclops has second drink, resulting in confusion

blocks.note: the setter, Cyclops, refers to himself as ME
S is the abbreviation for second
to sup is to drink

explanation.surface: The setter has another drink and things get muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming themselves in a clue usually stands for ME or I.
explanation.definitionFit: A mess-up is a muddle or bungle, so it describes a state of disorder and mistakes.

clue.text: Ghastly Gove's just started getting on edge

indicators.note: what has only just started has only its beginning showing, so take the opening letter

blocks.note: Michael Gove, a Conservative cabinet minister; his initial
a rim is an edge

explanation.surface: Horrible Michael Gove has only just begun to feel nervous.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On edge' looks like a phrase meaning nervous, but 'edge' is a piece on its own.
explanation.definitionFit: Grim and ghastly are synonyms, both describing something dreadful, bleak and unpleasant to face.

clue.text: Clue ending: 'nuts' – pardon?

indicators.note: something nuts is crazy, so the letters go wild and rearrange

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A baffled solver reads the last word of a clue and asks to hear it again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pardon?' looks like 'say again'; here it is the noun meaning remission.
explanation.definitionFit: In Catholic tradition an indulgence was a remission of punishment for sin granted by the Church, a kind of pardon.

clue.text: Blunt: his specialism is doing a U-turn in a sense

blocks.note: surface reading: someone named Blunt, a person who goes in for reversals

blocks.clueFragment: his specialism is doing a U-turn in a sense
blocks.note: setter's reading: the opposite of turning back is going directly ahead, a hint at the word for frank

explanation.surface: A man named Blunt is known above all for changing direction.
explanation.walkthrough: The blunt adjective means frank. The rest points to Tory MP Crispin Blunt, who left his marriage and came out as gay in 2010, a reversal of sorts.
explanation.definitionFit: Blunt and straight both describe frank, direct speech that avoids evasion; the word also means heterosexual, the joke's other sense.

clue.text: Adequate look over Brenda in list

indicators.note: turned over means flipped, so in a down clue the word reads upwards
'in' puts things inside another word, which then surrounds them

blocks.note: lo is an old word for look, as in 'lo and behold'
Brenda is Private Eye's nickname for Queen Elizabeth, whose cipher is ER
a table is a list of figures or names

explanation.surface: Someone checks over a woman called Brenda on a roster and finds her merely acceptable.
explanation.walkthrough: Private Eye calls the late Queen 'Brenda', and ER (Elizabeth Regina) is her royal cipher.
explanation.definitionFit: Tolerable means fairly good or bearable, just acceptable, the same middling standard as adequate.

clue.text: see 5dn.
Some ham actor's last meeting with actor Jane

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter, which alone is kept

blocks.note: the closing letter of the word
Jane Asher, the English actress

explanation.surface: A hammy performer's final scene is shared with the actress Jane Asher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ham actor' looks like one phrase about overacting, but 'Some ham' is the definition and 'actor's last' is a single letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A rasher is a thin slice of bacon or ham, so it is a portion of the meat.

clue.text: Terrible shape, full of shit – and so ends up on this?

definitions.note: the definition leans on the whole clue: what is in terrible shape ends up here

indicators.note: something terrible is in a bad way, so the letters are knocked into a new order
to be full of something is to hold it inside, so one piece wraps another

blocks.note: the word's letters rearranged
a vulgar synonym for excrement

explanation.surface: Something wrecked and rubbish is fit only for being thrown out.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters split around the inserted vulgarity; the closing words loop back to the whole clue for their sense.
explanation.definitionFit: A scrap heap is a pile of discarded junk, where anything worn out and worthless is finally dumped.

clue.text: Complaint: medical department running smoothly!

blocks.note: a complaint is an illness, such as flu
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department of a hospital

explanation.surface: A grievance about a hospital department that is, surprisingly, working well.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Complaint' suggests a grievance; in crosswords it often means an ailment.
explanation.definitionFit: Fluent speech or movement flows easily without hesitation or stumbling, which is what running smoothly describes.

clue.text: Pastry needs salt permit (about time)

indicators.note: 'about' means around, so the outer pieces go round the inner one

blocks.note: a salt and a tar are both old words for a sailor
T is the abbreviation for time
to let is to permit

explanation.surface: A baker needs a licence to use salt in a pastry, and there's a time limit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salt' looks like the seasoning but means a sailor; the joined sailor and permit go around time.
explanation.definitionFit: A tartlet is a small pastry case with a filling, so it is one kind of pastry.

clue.text: On one's deathbed – former Covid alert has taken one, right?

indicators.note: something that has taken things in now holds them inside itself

blocks.note: an ex is a former partner, so EX means former
the NHS Covid app 'pinged' contacts telling them to isolate
I is the Roman numeral one
R is the abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: A dying patient wonders whether the old Covid warning has claimed a victim.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2021 the NHS app's alert to self-isolate was called being 'pinged', the 'pingdemic'.
explanation.definitionFit: Expiring means breathing one's last, dying, which is the state of someone lying on a deathbed.

clue.text: Boris, before being associated with appalling mire

definitions.note: Boris Johnson, then the UK's prime minister: a definition by example

indicators.note: something appalling is a terrible state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: pre- is the prefix meaning before
the word's letters rearranged

explanation.surface: Boris Johnson, in his earlier days, linked with a dreadful swamp of scandal.
explanation.walkthrough: Boris Johnson was Britain's prime minister when this ran, so his first name stands for the title.
explanation.definitionFit: Premier is another word for prime minister, the office Johnson held, so he is an example of one.

clue.text: Consort's potty, after rinse

indicators.note: potty is British slang for crazy, so the letters go haywire

blocks.note: the two words taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A royal spouse's chamber pot gets used once it's been washed out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Consort' looks like a noun, a royal spouse, and 'potty' like a child's toilet; both are traps.
explanation.definitionFit: To consort with people is to associate with them socially, and fraternising means mixing on friendly terms.

clue.text: Inserting drug into that depraved character

indicators.note: depraved means corrupted, so the letters are perverted out of their order
inserting means putting one thing inside another

blocks.note: the word's letters rearranged
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: Someone slips drugs into a corrupt person's possession.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depraved character' reads as one wicked person, but 'character' alone is the definition: a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Theta is the eighth letter of the Greek alphabet, and character is a standard word for a written letter.

clue.text: see 5dn.
US political campaign organisation wants end to the controversial England and Wales legislation

definitions.text: the controversial England and Wales legislation

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that is taken

blocks.note: a PAC is an American political action committee
the closing letter of the word

explanation.surface: An American lobbying group demands the scrapping of a disputed English and Welsh law.
explanation.walkthrough: PACE is the Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984, which governs police powers in England and Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The acronym names the 1984 statute setting rules for police stop, search, arrest and detention.

clue.text: Whip holds Davey back – "he's not yet ready for command"

definitions.text: he's not yet ready for command

indicators.note: going back means travelling in the opposite direction, so the letters run backwards
to hold something is to have it within your grasp, so one piece encloses another

blocks.note: the cat-o'-nine-tails was a whip
Ed Davey, leader of the Liberal Democrats

explanation.surface: A party whip restrains Ed Davey, judging him unfit to lead.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whip' looks like a party disciplinarian, but it is the cat, a lash.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a trainee officer in the armed forces or police, still learning before taking command.

clue.text: Let yourself down with a book about fake news items?

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: taken as written
B is the abbreviation for book
fake news consists of falsehoods

explanation.surface: Disgrace yourself by publishing a book about misinformation.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Let yourself down' suggests disappointing people; it is literal, lowering yourself on a rope.
explanation.definitionFit: To abseil is to descend a cliff or wall on a rope, literally lowering your own body downward.

clue.text: Grant's stupid opening hint before climax

indicators.note: an opening is a beginning, so take only the first letter

blocks.note: the first letter of the word
a tip is a hint
the end is the climax or culmination

explanation.surface: Someone named Grant makes a foolish chat-up line in the lead-up to sex.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Grant' poses as a man's name; it is the noun for a sum of money awarded.
explanation.definitionFit: A stipend is a fixed regular allowance or salary, such as one given to a student or clergy, much like a grant.

clue.text: Peer (rat!) crudely grabbing end of amenable Oscar Wilde's thing

indicators.note: done crudely means roughly, without order, so the letters are knocked about
the end of a word is its final letter, the only one kept
to grab is to seize and hold, so one piece takes another inside it

blocks.note: the letters of both words rearranged
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: A lord, branded a rat, coarsely seizes something belonging to an obliging Oscar Wilde.
explanation.walkthrough: Wilde was celebrated for his quick-fire wit, so 'his thing' points to clever retorts.
explanation.definitionFit: Repartee is quick witty conversation full of clever replies, the trademark of Oscar Wilde's plays and dinner talk.

clue.text: Standing politician's against unprincipled Trump's election introductions

indicators.note: introductions come at the start, so take each word's opening letter

blocks.note: a rep, short for representative, is a US congressional politician
the first letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A sitting politician opposes Trump's shady election campaign.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing' looks like a politician standing for office; it means reputation.
explanation.definitionFit: Repute and standing both mean the regard or reputation in which someone is held by others.
